Author: @veracityseven
Content: To easily sum up the problem with the trucking industry.  2018: Pay per mile for a dry van = $2.10.  In 2025: Pay per mile for a dry van = $2.10.  Factor in the tremendous amount of inflation during that time and that results in a 38-40% decrease in pay...in just 8 years.  The 90% turnover rate is not a symptom of the problem so much as it is a way to continue eroding the industry.  New drivers expect, and receive, low wages.  When the onerous reality of the job sets in, and they come to the understanding that even some of the most experienced drivers are only making marginally more money...they quit.  Which allows/forces these huge carriers to continue the cycle. Unless there is some type of regulation that provides a modicum of prerequisites to obtaining a CDL, the industry will continue to deteriorate.

Author: @2TrackMind-c6i
Content:
There IS a driver shortage - and - there IS a shortage of good driving jobs.  The problem in the industry is systemic - from end to end.

I recently retired from a good, local driving job that was Unionized.  So, I have a pension and I had better tan average pay, vacation sick leave, etc. My company is a small carrier that has about 80 trucks.  Our turnover was almost non-existent.

I say all this to show that - even tho it was a good job at a good company, we could NOT get qualified drivers - period.  Our Hiring sign was a permanent fixture at the driveway.  Prospect after prospect failed either the drug test, the physical, or the driver record.  Virtually NO guys younger than 40 even applied.  The few females that applied and qualified washed out the first month due to the physical demands of our loads (flat bed, curtain vans...and not the best condition - you had to be strong).

So, my take away is:
1) Young people have little work ethic
2) Females can't do the work
3) Everyone is either on drugs or is a diabetic, or has high  blood pressure.

THAT"S why there is a driver shortage.

Content: Watching this while im sitting in my truck at the Walmart DC in Johnstown lmaooo 😂😅 I work for Swift (unfortunately) but they do have their own mini terminal inside of the Walmart DC. It is partially why these companies that hire new drivers can never seem to keep them. The payoff just really isnt worth it for a lot of people. Author: @orivalx
Content:
I am someone who works on the supply side of things specifically ive worked as the person signing cheques for the 3PLs in the permian basin. And this was insanely accurate and a fantastic video.

I will say there is a few things that were missed that I feel are important.

1: owner ops are paid well.
The rates generally go at 10$ per mile and go up by 2$ a mile every 10 miles. (Generally) so 0-10 is 10$ a mile
11-20 is 12$ per mile etc.

Most loads are between 40-60 miles.

We have a set time to unload in (90 mins) and if we exceed that then we have to pay 2$ per minute until the truck is unloaded.

Trucks take $1200 a day to run, so if a trucker isnt making that much at least they are losing money.

Owner ops are generally paid 70-80% of the amount we pay the 3PL company for a load.

Contract drivers always get fucked. And its very common for them to work in standard 3PL companies. Which felt like the opposite was implied here. On a job generally only 30-50% were owner ops.

Author: @mmoly-cj4bd
Content: Being white collar and college educated when I was working my way down the ladder, I got my CDL and began driving for SWIFT in 2010 over-the-road. All I got paid was .29 per mile.  I made about 28K my first 12 months on the job. There was no extra compensation for anything else period. I did deliveries for Walmart driving their equipment for about a week on a contract arraignment with SWIFT. I made deliveries to stores in the Phoenix area on a daily daylight hour basis. At SWIFT I worked 12 days on then 2 days off. You can't really buy food and it's hard to pay your bills or enjoy any down time. One thing many people don't know is that coming off you off days you could get a trip that doesn't start until the evening and you pretty much ending up taking trips for two weeks where you are driving overnight and then trying to sleep the next day. That's very hard to do. Also, some truck stops are in some bad parts of cities. I was also very good at trip planning but sometimes you just get stuck with a trip with lousy drive times and delivery and/or pickup points where it can be very challenging trying to get into a shopping center or urban location. I think the average driver turnover rate at the time was 6 mos. I lasted 15 months. I think the lesson that I learned was that you have to find a way through brains to figure out how to have control over your life. You have to care about yourself first and foremost because nobody else will.  That was the life lesson perhaps I needed to learn from driving a semi around the country. Although I was a great driver, I can honestly say that this was the worst job I ever had. I have a lot of respect for the man or women behind the wheel of large trucks. I also feel sad for them at the same time.

Author: @johnniewelbornjr.8940
Content:
I am approaching my 32nd year of holding a CDL and I think I've been trying to escape driving for 31 years.  lol  I started off in cabovers with one of the big dry-van companies back in 1993 (now long gone) and moved on to steel-hauling and tankers and, finally, heavy-haul (oversized/overweight loads, including two years of windmill blades).  Now back in a winch truck in the North Dakota/Montana/Wyoming oilfields (sadly, it pays far better than windmill blades, which is completely backwards) and home 99% of my nights.  I remember better days in the industry but it was already beginning to decline even by the time I started.  I've been in all of the "lower 48" states and even used to go into Ontario and Quebec back in the 90s...  More recently, running permitted loads with specified routing from each state, I've seen some extremely remote, out-of-the-way places due to the "zig/zag" nature of such routes that avoid road construction zones or low clearances/low weight limits (we often joked that a Texas permit to get from Houston to Dallas might route one via El Paso, for example lol).  Some of the routes up and down the Plains and Rockies region are so familiar that I even recall potholes (sad  lol) or, worse, recognize things like the Pilot in Orla, Texas that's in this video.  

It's been a job...  That's all I can say for it all.  There's none that's perfect.  I certainly DON'T encourage anyone to get their CDL, though, for there are a lot of downsides, especially as a beginner.  But, even so, it IS what one makes of it, too.  Some love it still...  But, for me, the thrill is gone.

Author: @Happymouth1
Content:
Gotta keep in mind that "$400/day" number is after 14 hours of work. 70hrs/week to clear $2k... That is a pretty good number if you got a good few loads and high CPM. But you're working double the time, sleeping on the road, showering in gas stations for essentially $28/hr.

They are also one of the hardest places to get a job at, you need to pass a lot of requirements on top of having a spotless record and over 2 years of Class A experience.

Trucking is also one of the highest regulated industries in USA, it is on par or even higher than the medical/hospital field. Your pre-trip/post-trip is something that if you skip it and something happens you are gonna be in a world of hurt. Legally, not just from your job. Roads (especially out east) are not designed for the 53ft trailers and 20ft sleeper cabs. Drivers will hate you, cut you off, or give you zero room, no matter what, weigh-ins and inspections can bog you down and risk fines, and on top of that companies will abuse the hell out of you.

I had high hopes when i got my CDL but tbh i don't think it is a good industry. If you're single or in a relationship where you both are OK with it, then its not so bad, you take in a lot of sights and just stay on the road and can earn some decent money. 100k-ish. But that turnover is no joke, a LOT of people, realize its not for them and quit before the end of their first year.

Content:
In my country, another thing contributing to this is the lack of trucking infrastructure. Truckers are just treated like anyone else using the road for a leasure trip. They get no dedicated infrastructure 
Most motorway service stations are built around cars, because a family on a long distance drive will spend more for the amenities at the service. So the things they should be for, trucks, are relegated to the back of the planners' minds. Truckers even have to pay out of pocket for a shower or to sleep in an actual bed overnight, neither the government or the companies compensate them for any of these necessary amenities, hell even going to the bathroom isn't free for many of them. And many don't even have places to park HGVs, or have max heights at the entrance only letting in cars and so on.

- Pre-trip inspections still need to be done by a person as well as checking tractor/trailer on the road.
- Trucks where drivers unload freight.
- Hazmat response to any damage or leak for haul.
- Dirt roads or damaged streets.

Author: @Baseball-huh01
Content:
My grandpa drove truck from 1972 to 2008. My dad drove truck from 1999 to 2024. My uncle drove truck from 1991 to 2019. My other uncle drove truck from 1987 to 2022. I drove truck from 2013 to 2022. 

My grandpa bought and paid his home off in 1978. He retired from the industry worth several million dollars because he got paid so well through most of his career he was able to invest in retirement and in the stock market. He cashed out of the market in late 07 and quit driving his truck when the price of diesel went up in 08. Keep in mind he started driving before deregulation and he always said “good damn thing I bought the house before Carter fkd me”. 

My oldest uncle, similar story, though more difficult for him, bought his house and paid it off in 1999. He continued to drive until his retirement and investments were enough to live on but again, he had the luck of being able to buy before the housing market shot up after 08. 

My younger uncle also got lucky that he bought his house before 08, paid it off in 2004. However, being able to retire wasn’t why he quit, granted he was getting close. He quit because rates had started falling hard. 

Me… I got started in trucking after 08 so houses were through the roof, I wound up taking a deal from a scumbag mobile home dealer paying almost double for a trailer house not even built as good as a dry van semi trailer - there was no saving for retirement, every dime I could put toward the mobile home went toward the mobile home. Thankfully I was able to pay it and the land it sits on off in 2022 and I quit trucking the very next day. Rates fell in 2019 and the pandemic screwed everything up even more. I was barely making anything. I was driving with two e-logs, unplugging one so I could run the second, 18 hours a day or more driving the truck just so I could bring home a couple grand a week. I did that shit for 2 1/2 years. I was tired. I was an owner operator, like under my own authority and everything. I built that for myself from 2013 to 2017. Freight started averaging fkn $2.50 a mile and that’s barely enough to keep the truck on the road in legal condition (so obviously I wasn’t fixing minor shit because I had to make money and eat too). 

One thing this video over looks is a factor that the internet doesn’t really like to speak about out loud - foreign drivers. Now, I’m not a conspiracy theorist, I don’t buy into the states just handing out non-domiciled CDLs to foreigners who can’t speak English shit. I do, though, believe that foreign drivers are far more willing to work for less money. I’ve seen it time and time again. These Arabs and Indians are willing to come over here and drive as a team running their trucks 24 hours a day driving the cheapest freight in brokerage history primarily because American citizens won’t take cheap freight because they have a life outside that truck to support and the foreigners really don’t. They’ll come in here and make all this money for a few years and then go back to wherever they came from. This, of course, isn’t the only American industry to have this issue. It happened to agriculture in the 70s with a massive influx of Mexican immigration. It happened to manufacturing up north with an influx of Irish immigration. I’m not saying these are all bad things because they’re just a natural part of any industry in a country like ours, I’m just saying this is why trucking is falling so hard. Rates fell in 2019 because of this. Rates fell during the pandemic because of this. Trucking felt this so late because truckers used to, as horrible as this sounds, gang up on these foreign nationals and force them “off the road” so to speak. I’m not calling for that to happen but I am calling for a few things:

1) enforce the English Only requirement of the FMCSA. A lot of these folks speak just enough English to pass the test but can’t hardly communicate past that. I’m not saying, again, that states are just handing these licenses out to people who can’t speak English, I’m saying they need to actually pass an English exam like people take in school. Drivers ought to have to be fluent. Airline pilots have to be fluent in English anywhere in the world.  Truckers in the U.S. and Canada should be too. 

2) cut the leasing programs. Drivers are either employees or independent contractors who own their own truck either out right or financed by an institution that has no involvement with any carrier. That middle ground of being an o/o while being treated like an employee needs to go. 

3) Relax the Hours of Service rules and make it a 16 hour day regardless of whether that’s driving or otherwise working and get rid of the requirement of a 34, of course for o/o only. O/Os have a business to run and money to make. 

4) for company drivers, 40 hours a week paid by the hour with mandatory overtime after 40 hours like any other job. Mandatory two days off per week, rotating between consecutive days off and split days off. Max of 16 hours a day but no more than 70 hours in one week. Must provide benefits to employees. “That’s bad for business”. Yeah a mega carrier can afford it though. Employees are people. If they wanted to be worked to death they’d be an o/o. 

5) no more speed limiters being demanded by insurance companies. Let these trucks run the posted speed limit. No separate speed limit for trucks, California. The faster they drive the more work they can get done and the less in the way they are of other vehicles. Sure trucks are the direct cause of fewer accidents by being slow but they’re the indirect cause of a plethora of accidents by being slow.

Content:
I have been driving for 5 years. 1.5 regional and 3.5 local delivery. For around a 20-30% pay cut i work 45 hours and have 4 day weeks (Tuesday-Friday.) Regional and OTR can pay better but you sacrifice a lot of your life for slightly higher earnings. 
If you are getting your CDL-A, NEVER get it through a company you will work for. You will have a 12-24 month window where if you quit you must repay the whole cost or it is pro-rated. Many companies have a tuition reimbursement plan paid over 12-18 months with no contract. 
The autonomous truck is mostly fan fiction. Automation works great in a controlled environment, not in the real world. Freight could be shut down for days or weeks in the case of bad weather. There are also many instances where human intuition and reactions cannot be replicated. It won't last long after a couple 80,000 lb vehicles smash into stopped vehicles on the interstate because the computer didnt stop in time. Plus you still have to park, back into docks, fuel, and drive in cities where you cannot use the street lines to maneuver.

Author: @InfamousScroller
Content:
For the independent drivers, it’s not 100% like you said.

I professionally worked for one of those companies. My company had one of the biggest fleets in the US, but I worked for their “Brokerage” division.

Basically, they fit different needs. We offered the ability to sell our “asset” fleet, which were trucks we owned, where they were full time and paid as employees, and we offered our “logistics brokerage services” where we brokered out loads to the highest bidder.

The thing to understand is, as someone who sold, managed, and found my own leads, a company that only ships one expensive load per shipment is never going to need their own fleet trucker, or an assigned asset trucker from a carrier, they’ll need a brokerage. This is for all one big time moves.

On the topic of XPO, you had one larger mistake here, they are primarily what is called LTL. (Less than truckload) this means they pick unless multiple companies products and pallets from multiple areas, and/or deliver them to multiple areas and companies. This is only cost effective where someone only needs 1-5 pallets shipped.

Also, when pricing out, port shipments are hard to broker. They require extra credentials and passes, they tend to have a lot of traffic and have a prepaid detention fee, and ANY MAJOR CITY port, adds like an extra $1,000 due to lack of drivers. 

When we are pricing out loads, it acts as a free market space where semi-truck drivers can negotiate their own rates depending on the lane, the load weight, and the pickup and drop off.

The big 4 types of delivery styles are LTL, Full Van, Flatbed, or whiteglove direct (sprinter vans)


Opendeck/flatbed heavyhaul tends to pay the most, but they are one time shipments.

And while you may think that LA port lane is “the worst” a lot of owner operators will take those due to wanting to work in a specific area and not wanting to do long hauls, so they specialize in their own regions. What this means is, the port carriers are overwhelmingly Asset or fleet drivers, paid a salary, not independent truckers who broker loads. The long distance truckers are a different breed.

On the topic of driver shortages, during covid there was a major one, because everyone shifted to ordering things online, which while last mile is parcel, still uses a lot of LTL and Full truckload pickups and deliveries on the shipping business to fedex etc, so the industry saw a large boom.

The biggest thing is, truckers who specialize make the most money, the brokered loads one have complete say in if they do or do not move, and the fleet driver jobs may be the best with benefits, but tend to make less money overall. 

The LEAST specialized job is an LTL trucker, as it is small business to business shipments all in one area. This is what XPO specializes in, hence the staggeringly low rates. 

For the oil, gas and dirt haulers, those are almost never brokered loads. They generally require specific equipment and company trucks, so they are 90% of the time company/asset/fleet drivers. So when you said “3pL companies and oil companies can bring in more owner operators”, it’s really just not the case. That is likely more an issue with between oil companies underpaying their own fleet drivers. There simply isn’t a large market for oil tanker owner operators. This is due to liability, and such. If I were selling them, I would price out monthly minimums as a dedicated lane.

Last but not least, we had an expensive paid for study for AI trucking and when to invest in an automated fleet, and basically, it won’t take off until the roads start having infrastructure built for automated cars and trucks. So it’s unlikely to change until the government adapts, which will be awhile.

Author: @rochester212
Content:
At my garage there are 3 toilets and 2 showers for 100+ truck drivers who essentially live in the trucks. The situation is common across Europe. This is even before starting to mention the actual working conditions, for example many companies force the driver to perform repairs on truck and trailer, fix flats, often without proper tools. You work at night, you work during the holidays. On ocassion you break the law, because the company wants to increase the profit margin.
Lots of laws and regulations are not followed, most common one is that although it's illegal to spend the weekly pause inside the cab, most cross-border truck drivers never leave the truck until they go on vacation. No authority in the European Union cares about the situation, but everybody knows what's going on. Even basic things, like finding a parking spot is a challenge, especially at the end of the week. How many truck drivers sleep at the side of the road every night across Europe we'il knever know, but if you do the math, the numbers would be staggering.
In conclusion, if you always wanted to be a cowboy in the Wild West, driving a truck is the closest you'il get to that in 2025.

Author: @ron6625
Content:
My father drove truck since he was 14 until he was about 65. It was the fashion at the time. 

He did just about everything, long haul, short haul, across all of NA. At around 45 he switched to an overnight route from Windsor to Toronto, and during days he would occasionally teach one on one road experience with the noobies.

During the ass end of his career, he really hated what the industry was evolving into. Trucks with automatic transmissions, guys who didn't learn/wouldn't learn proper load securement. Guys who didn't properly do their inspections. He was pretty frustrated with it all.

But he loved driving truck. It saved him when he was young when he was tossed out at 13 to fend for himself. But jt cost him too. 

My mother is nuts. He married her while she was young. He gave her everything,  treated her well. But he was never home. She took off and left him. I  rarely got to see him growing up. A few summers in my early years, and then nothing during the rough ones. I resented him for it. 

But as dark as everything was during that time, when I grew into a man myself, I had good memories of what love looked like from the few memories I had with my father. Those memories I think were huge in preventing me from going down the same path as my mother. So even though he wasn't there, he still had a big impact on my life.

This profession, love it or hate it: these men make big sacrifices in order to make it work. Women are now getting more involved in the industry too, and I have nothing but respect for truckers. Just try to find some time to spend with your kids eh? The money is important, but you won't regret missing work to spend time with your kids when   your time is up.

Author: @OnceDrivenForeverSmitten
Content:
Interesting video. Not sure about fully automated trucks with no drivers becoming a reality though. The tech will exist to do it but there's more to the job than merely going from one point to another. 

Trucking isn't going driverless in Europe. Maybe it would work sending something from A to B on a deserted Interstate but the role of the driver here in the UK anyway extends way beyond simply piloting the truck to its destination. 

Surely only the most basic and mundane driving jobs would be lost to driverless trucks in the USA. If it was the likes of Amazon trying it the trucks would be targeted by thieves. It'd be easy to get it to stop in the middle of nowhere. Or they'd be jumping into the trucks on the move, breaking in and launching stuff out.

European roads are so often clogged with traffic there are situations where you cannot pull out on a roundabout or junction without someone letting you out, or just pulling out and making traffic slow or stop. An automated truck can't make eye contact with another driver who is waving them out, they could end up stuck at places for ages. Badly parked cars could mean the only option is to drive up onto a pavement or onto a verge. Getting AI to take these technically illegal actions or calculated risks is difficult.

When it comes to loading or unloading there's the matter of going to find the right part of a site, the right person who deals with it and securing the load, which is the responsibility of the driver who is then usually liable should something happen as a result. 

Numerous motorway closures and complicated diversions are also very common in the UK. Drivers aren't going anywhere. It's an essential industry but one which the government neither understands nor cares about they aren't currently treating it with the outright contempt they do farming but give it time.

Content:
I've worked for both a freighttech startup looking to disrupt the industry (it didn't) and an older school trucking and warehousing company.

The thing you neglected to mention is the impact of insurance on the whole boondoggle. It's cost prohibitive for O-Os, but also for smaller carriers. As a result, smaller companies can generally only employ drivers who have several years of driving under their belts because their insurance requires them to. So who do you work for if you're just starting out? Companies that can afford the insurance premiums for new drivers. Wal-Mart. Amazon. None of which are known for sharing their wealth with the people that create it.

Author: @RyaansInSpace
Content:
Not a trucker personally but I work in parts sales at a semi dealership and have a few observations. 

Parts prices (much like everything else) have been steadily rising, especially on parts for newer motors. A turbo for a 2021+ runs anywhere from $7-9k. 

Truck sales themselves have gone way down. Fleet customers that would buy 70-80 trucks annually or semi-annually have cut those orders in half or skipped ordering trucks altogether. 

It’s become a lot harder to be an owner/operator with these rising prices, and we see it every day which customers are financially responsible and are able to keep working, and which ones are forced to park their trucks while they wait for prices to come down to even be able to repair their rigs or even make it worth driving. 

The tariffs, specifically on the US/Mexico border, are no joke and we hear stories about the uptick in import charges and fees for customers who run back & forth.

Content: When I did professional driving I got paid per load. No mileage, no hookup pay, no delivery/stop pay, no delay pay, and no layover pay. The company paid all tolls so no money for crossing a bridge, no pay for breakdowns, no pay while waiting for a load, and no benefits. That was twenty some odd years ago and that was the industry standard. They had GPS in the vehicles, but the dispatchers could only see where someone was at, at any given moment. And the drivers knew how to defeat the system. The hours were horrendous because drivers were fudging their books just to make minimum wage. Some drivers were even using more than one book, all of which would eventually result in mandated electronic log books. Suddenly drivers were making even less pay resulting in people leaving the profession for other jobs that paid more. Pay at most companies is ridiculously low when compared to the actual hours, it's hard work, and destroys a person's health. Add mistreatment by dispatchers... is it any wonder the turn over is so high?

Author: @ultmateragnarok8376
Content:
Driverless trucking is kind of a joke. In a mostly-controlled environment where very little changes, you can get successful runs, but contending with the immensely vast number of factors that create unpredictable situations on the road is something you couldn't get a truck to reliably do on its own even if the whole trailer was one big computer. Even the rail industry, without having any worry about things like being cut off by other drivers or keeping between dubiously maintained lane markings, has continuously failed in its struggle to automate the running of vehicles. You can build a dedicated track, or a dedicated road, with enough effort and money, and run your autonomous vehicle on that, but by that point you might as well just pay the drivers to do it instead. And in many industries you run further into issues with loading and unloading needing similarly unrealistic optimizations just to keep up with trucks that can theoretically drive 24/7. Maintenance is also a whole other problem - with no driver to check on each and every vehicle, they will encounter issues and eventually outright break down, meaning you need a similar workforce anyways. The automation simply doesn't exist, and attempts have shown little promise, while the theoretical success outpaces the other components of the system it is intended to work within.
This is not to claim there aren't many important improvements to the drivers' experience that can be made with computer assistance. But the control and sight this gives the companies above those workers is a steep price to pay, and replacing the human in the equation is simply not an option for the forseeable future.

Author: @libertasaeterna5365
Content: I am sand hauler (company driver) in the permian. Everything he said is true and worse!! What appealed to me about the oilfield was the 21/7 schedule that allows me to see my pregnant girlfriend more often. I came from OTR making a consistent 1300-1500 a week. But the pay in sand hauling can vary   wildly. Our company wants 2 loads a day, which on paper doesn't seem that hard but it's the bottlenecks that can happen during those loads. The sand plant is constantly going down, or something may happen at the well. I've sat for 6 hours before waiting on sand, then get to the well, and had to wait another 5 hours because the frac went down. I have pulled 21 hour days just to get two loads in. On a good week, I can make 1300-1700. That's nothing going wrong and a consistent 2 loads a day.on a bad week, I've had $600 checks. I love that 7 days off though, if we were compensated even a bare minimum for the sitting time it would make the industry better. I can tell you trucking can save lives. As long as your license isn't fucked up you can go from being homeless and as long as you keep your bills low you can pull yourself out of a dark place. Trucking and Oil are the only industries I know where a few weeks of training you can go make a half decent salary even if you have a criminal record.

Author: @JR_MacD
Content:
I drove OTR for 2.5 years. I made $0.61 per mile at my last  job. (J&R Schugel) and I yuy treated well enough. Land Air (Covenant subsidiary) before that at $0.60 per mile. Again, treated pretty well by the company. 

"Thr Probelm" with trucking doesnt exist. It's "The Laundry List of Problems".

I am only ~5 minutes into the vid, but heres what i sa:

1- race to the bottom by the mega-carriers (Schneider, Swift, et al). In normal corporate shittery, those carriers did their best maximize the number of loads, they competed by lowering their freight rates for contracted customers.

2- In lowering their rates, they still needed to maximize profites, with only one knob to turn: lower driver pay.

3- By lowering the rates so much, Owner/Operators were forced to acquiesce to the rates. Load boards (and fucking brokers) helped force the price drop.

4 - States, counties, etc have completely dropped the ball with way too few trucker reat stops and facilities for sleeping, etc. Most drivers avoid on ramp and off ramp stops, but there simply aren't enough legal places to stop, especially on the coasts. (I-95 corridor, Im looking at you!)

5 - Since government agencies dropped the ball, its left to corporations like Love's, Pilot, etc, to provide truck stops with  legal places to stop. Butbthat requires that the truck stop is a viable business. Good luck making a 5-10 acre truck stop profitable in places like southern California. (So you end up with only 3 or 4 truck stops between Los Angeles and Palm Springs)

6 - With job "pain" getting worse and worse, you get massive driver turn over, often with the onky ones sticking it out being the ones with no choice, and often crap drivwra. Not to mention the massive number of rookies (me included) that makes things more dangerous.

ELDs are ok, imho. While they are a pain, they make it much more difficult for shit companies to force drivers into bad situations. If truking companies weren't so notoriously shit, paper logs would still be the rule. (At least at smaller outfits, mega corps would still use them to micromanage their drivers)

The tl;dr? Corporate profiterring and government failing to update/upgrade trucking infrastructure are the big problems.

But hey, those mega-mansions and yachts dont pay for themselves!

Author: @darthrainbows
Content:
Self-driving trucks are such an obvious win for everyone except the teamsters themselves that their deployment en-mass is inevitable. How fast that happens is of course an open question, but probably depends a lot on how expensive it is to retrofit an existing truck to full self-driving capability and how much an operator actually saves by not having to pay a driver.

Imagine that Walmart was to replace the example driver with an autonomous truck, and the cost savings for the labor of the driver are half of the driver's daily wages. That saves $70,000/year. Then, the truck can operate 24/7 without breaks, so Walmart can handle the same volume of shipping with fewer physical trucks, or ship more with the same number of trucks, adding onto the savings. The trucks should be safer as well, reducing the costs of insuring them and the potential for damages in the event of an accident... The cost savings keep piling up. Some of this will be offset by the need to employ people to handle things like the safety checks, fueling/charging the trucks, etc. but most of that is already handled by not offsetting the full wages paid to the driver. If my napkin-math is anything close to reality, there is practically no refit cost that isn't worth paying to convert the whole fleet over immediately. Heck, they could purchase brand new trucks (often $300000+ each, with half a million not being out of reach) and scrap the entire existing fleet and it would *still* be a great investment.

Content:
Was a part time local trucker for 6 months a few years back! It wasn't long but I learned so much about the industry in just that little time and honestly I loved the job. I loved the job, but from what I hear the whole industry is like that, and I just can't do that. Great job, great coworkers, even a cool fleet manager, but having to deal with weight limits and them not even trying to keep my weight under annoyed me so much.

Author: @mnshp7548
Content:
In my mind, truck driving is one of those jobs where you get to sit in a climate-controlled cab all day, listening to music while getting paid to drive. It's not the hardest job to do—most people could probably learn to drive a truck if they really wanted to. Sure, it's not for everyone, but I personally don't see it as a highly specialized skill. That said, I’m not putting truckers down. I get that it can be mentally draining—sitting for hours, waiting around at depots, and trying to navigate tight city streets in rush hour sounds rough.

But at the end of the day, you’re just in a truck. You’re not performing surgery or breaking your back in a warehouse for 12+ hour shifts on even lower pay. If anything, bus drivers arguably deserve more money, since they're responsible for the safety of multiple people every single day—kids, commuters, the lot.

Also, from an efficiency standpoint, trucks aren’t great. Trains could handle large volumes of deliveries more effectively, cutting down traffic and improving delivery times since they’re not stuck in congestion. It’s the kind of system that makes more sense in the long run.

Unfortunately, like many manual jobs—leather work, heavy labour, etc.—I feel like truck driving might not have a long future. With autonomous vehicles and smarter logistics coming in, it’s probably one of those roles that will slowly disappear or shift massively, and I feel sorry for any trucker out there that enjoys their line of work, but cant continue due to the cost of doing it.

Author: @PeteDriver530
Content: former driver (1992-2005, lease operator 1997-2000), whenever someone asks why I quit and my stock answer is always "it quit being fun or profitable".  while this is an extreme generalization, there is a lot of truth in it.  over those 13 years I watched the traffic get worse, the law enforcement get out of hand, and the price of fuel go through the roof, not to mention the 'quality' of drivers the trucking schools were shoveling out.  and with the looming doom of electronic logs, DEF and in-cab cameras, I realized this was no longer an industry for a 'diesel pilot' who could get out there and drive.  it quite literally (for myself at least but I know a few others) went from doing something I loved and was good at to being joyless work that practically forbade you from doing your job to the best of your skills and abilities.  it's been almost 20 years since I last stepped down from the cab, and yes there are parts of it I do miss but it's highly unlikely that I would go back to it.  while "it's not like it was" is rather cliche it is accurate and I'm still not sure if I felt I couldn't adapt to the changes or just refused to, the outcome is the same and I feel no regrets.  I read the other day that Kenworth is going to stop making the W900 and Peterbilt is doing the same with the 389 meaning the era of long square hood trucks is coming to an end after so many decades, and it makes me sad.  in a way it parallels how my driving career ended, with a casual "we're gonna do things 'different & better' and we don't need you anymore" situation.  so there's my two cents, take a penny leave a penny.  thanks to Wendover for a great video, and y'all be safe out there!

Truck drivers were making more PROFIT than ever before during the pandemic. They were regularly getting paid $4+/mi and fully paid out for all accessorial fees like detention, layover, etc. AND at inflated rates. 

It’s why we see a boom in the amount of MC’s registered with the FMSCA during this same time period. 

Anyone that tries to tell you truck drivers had a tough time during the pandemic is quite frankly full of shit. Drivers will try to dramatize it and make it seem like it was a tough time, all the while sitting back with a grin on their face knowing the level of profit margin they were making. And truck drivers are VERY good at making a lot of fuss on social media, etc, so every news article you see trying to throw pitty on truck drivers for how the market is currently - just know these guys were making BANK during the pandemic when most people struggled. 

This is coming from a Logistics Management Consultant who works with both carriers AND shippers. My viewpoint is from a completely neutral perspective.

Author: @tyhutson6558
Content:
I’ve been a Logistics Management Consultant for over a decade and I’ll sum this up very simply.

The problem with the logistics industry that we’ve seen especially over the past 5 years is the mass influx of visa-affiliated drivers who have no formal training and don’t speak any English. They book loads for cheap and it seems appealing at first to many companies but it has severally cut back on efficiency - costing shippers money in the long term. Everything is a snowball effect in logistics. 

I talk to about 20 drivers a day on average, and maybe 3-5 of them can speak/understand English or know the rules/regs. Trucking companies hire these drivers because they’re able to pay them far less than a properly trained driver. I’ll leave you with this, over the past 5 years - Non-English, foreign sourced drivers account for roughly 80% of all fatalities from accidents involving truck drivers. The problem is right in front of us but no one wants to say it because you’re “racist/xenophobic” if you do. We need to stop jeopardizing efficiency and the safety of everyone on the road and require much stricter guidelines for the type of people that are allowed to drive a truck. Period.

Author: @andersonklein3587
Content: Obviously automation will worsen the situation for truckers, because it will reduce demand for workers. In the long term though it unlocks further capital density per worker. The ultimate truth for any sector of the economy, be it the underpaid food, farm labor, warehouse, or even some office job types, is that there are too many workers. The market is flooded with desperate applicants and companies can just pick and choose who to hire and at what terms. This won't change until there is either a massive increase in capital investments, or a demographic shift reducing the labor pool. Both of those are very slow processes played over decades, and will fight an uphill battle against automation and immigration. While workers are still likely to be slightly better off in the medium term, the reality of it is that our societies have been energy starved since the late 1960s and we are still paying societal interest on the massive baby boom of the 20th century. What capital holders see as demographic dividends, cheap abundant labor, is truly exactly what is described, being forced to work for low wages with little bargaining power.

Content:
I am an owner operator with a trucking authority. I am sorry to say but the video missed the mark completely. 

The story it tells firstly is  very unorganized, from Walmart to XPO, to Owner Operators. Ughhh just messy. 

Secondly is how detached media and reporting is in regard to trucking. Whoever did this research just surfed the web for narratives, and articles and tried to build a story from that.

They can install double or triple the premium if you give them the reason to. 

4. The legacy manufacturers are becoming more and more expensive and less and less driver friendly. 

They have become increasingly more greedy. The keep information and repair data proprietary and the dealers are the only ones that can fix the problem. Costing poor drivers tens of thousands on repairs that once costed a few 100. 

They practice planned obsolescence and purposely build trucks to lose their value fast. Trucks these days are disposable rather than reliable. 

Cummins, Paccar, Daimler, Volvo North America, Navistar International, all do this. 

5. The freight industry, brokers, shippers, receivers, middle men, freight boards. Have little to no regulation. 

6. Out federal and state governments have all but stoped their support to further develop parking infrastructure and improve the road. 

7. Fraud is rampant.

Author: @Chud-Tungsten
Content:
Funny how the same people who are for regulating domestic industries are gaslit to be against regulating global trade so easily.  An unregulated market is always dominated by the entity that grows to the correct scale for maximizing dominance while minimizing internal logistics friction AND manages to offload costs onto the public & contractors while retaining profits for itself. 

 In this regard, there's no difference between domestic & global markets.  3rd world industry offloads many of the costs globally (particularly pollution), but retains the profits of industry within its borders.  Competing against countries with living standards far below the 1st means any 1st country is almost entirely limited to competing in the "premium" or "luxury" goods portion of any market that can be globalized via shipping.

Is this more efficient overall?  In the short term... yes.  In the long term no.  In the very long term... maybe.  Depends on how long it takes for 2nd/3rd world industry to achieve 1st world status & living standards & how much damage & degradation the 1st world suffers in the interim.

Overall, 1st world countries offshoring industry to the 2nd/3rd world is an act of greed in the short term, an act of self-flagellating charity in the long term, and maybe net neutral in the best case long term scenario.

It's absurd that our weak perception of consequence over time has been manipulated to convince us to screw ourselves so easily.

My dad was a technician in an oil refinery. One of his jobs involved trucks taking product away to be delivered to gas stations.

It's also a sad fact that that the US trucking hardware is woefully outdated. All the tech is basically stuck in the 70's when it comes to driver comfort and safety, and even the modern engines are old and inefficient when compared to regular european stuff.

And with that, more improvements can be made to the loads themselves. Take finland for example, the maximum vehicle combination length is just 34,5 metres (113 feet), but the maximum weight of such combination at 8 axles is 64 metric tonnes (141 000 pounds). Scale that up to 11 axles and the maximum weight is 76 tonnes (167 500 pounds). The US gross weight limit is just 80 000 pounds (36 tonnes) even at 6 axles, whereas in finland that would be 53 tonnes (116 800 pounds).

Author: @aaronvandyck5837
Content:
Really insightful video. The situation in the U.S. closely mirrors what's happening in Western Europe. Over here, the industry isn’t necessarily oversaturated, but it's under heavy pressure due to a steady influx of cheap labor from Eastern Europe. Large transport companies are taking full advantage of this, which has driven down wages and working conditions for Western European drivers.

Many Eastern European truckers are employed through loopholes like letterbox companies or posted worker schemes, often working for weeks or months on end, underpaid and living in poor conditions. This results in social dumping and unfair competition, while making the job increasingly unattractive for local drivers.

It seems the trucking industry—on both sides of the Atlantic—is stuck in a model that exploits drivers rather than values them.

Author: @micahbonewell5994
Content:
The problem with Autonomous trucks overtaking the trucking industry is that Autonomous trucking would require, either 1: contractor businesses to grow up which own the expensive trucks, pay for the gas and maintain the trucks, not to mention cover the liability of anytime a truck breaks down or causes an accident. Or more business to become like Walmart and maintain their own fleets (which seems to be the minority at the moment).

Option 1 runs counter to everything you just described in the video. Companies like XPO Logistics, instead of running lean on capital, would have to buy and maintain a large fleet of trucks (investing in a large staff of mechanics), they would have to ensure they were positioned well rather than calling on a large pool of available truckers. This would then make them carry the burden of delays, large gas costs, trucks breaking down to likely mismanagement and so on.

Author: @leandervr
Content:
This kind of fake independency has been made illegal in the Netherlands. If you are de facto dependant on a company, they are obliged to offer you a contract with full benefits. Simple logic is that the law won't treat you as independent if you are not independent. Logistics was the biggest area where this was an issue too, the biggest delivery company PostNL was working with a ton of "independent" van drivers who had their own van, all maintenance costs for themselves, which also let them exceed maximum working hours. Forcing your own workers to work more than 40 hours is basically impossible and you have to pay a lot to get them to do it, but of course if you are independent you can work as many hours as you want, you are your own boss... 

We really are still a capitalist country, but you have to regulate stuff like this! Come US, your truckers deserve this. (No chance in Trump's US though I bet...)
